The noun loafer has two completely different meanings in English. You need to know both, because native speakers use both regularly.

A loafer is a person who avoids work and spends their time doing nothing useful. They are idle, unproductive, and unwilling to put in effort. Think of someone who lies on a couch all day, skips their responsibilities, and lets others carry the load.

The word carries a mildly negative, disapproving tone. It's not a harsh insult, but it is a criticism. When someone calls another person a loafer, they mean: this person is wasting their time and not contributing.

Examples in sentences:

  • "Don't be a loafer — get up and help with the chores."
  • "He was known as the neighborhood loafer, always sitting outside while everyone else went to work."
  • "Her boss warned her that loafers had no place on his team."

The key idea is habitual laziness. A loafer isn't just someone who rested on one particular day — it's a person whose default mode is idleness. It's a part of their character, not a single incident.

A loafer is also a specific style of shoe. This is probably the more commonly encountered meaning in everyday modern life.

Here is what defines a loafer as a shoe:

It has no laces, buckles, or straps to fasten. You simply slide your foot in and out — no tying, no adjusting. This is the single most important feature. Because of this, loafers are sometimes called slip-on shoes.

They are flat or low-heeled. Loafers sit close to the ground. They do not have a raised heel like boots or heels. This makes them comfortable for extended wear.

They are typically made from leather or suede, though modern versions also come in canvas or synthetic materials. The classic loafer has a neat, clean appearance.

They cover the top of the foot (unlike sandals) but do not go up the ankle (unlike boots). They are similar in coverage to a regular sneaker or Oxford dress shoe.
What Does a Loafer Look Like?

Imagine a smooth, closed shoe. The top of the shoe (the part that covers the foot) is usually one continuous piece of material without any opening or flap. Across the front — roughly where the toes meet the arch of the foot — there is a horizontal strap or band stitched onto the shoe. This strap is decorative and structural, and it gives the loafer its distinctive, recognizable look.

This strap can be plain, or it can carry a decorative element. This is where the different types of loafers come from:

  • Penny loafer: The strap has a small diamond-shaped slot cut into it. Traditionally, people slipped a penny coin into that slot — hence the name. This is the most classic, iconic loafer style.
  • Tassel loafer: The strap has small tassels (little decorative fabric or leather knots) hanging from it.
  • Horsebit loafer: The strap carries a metal horse-bit ornament (a U-shaped piece of metal with a bar across it). This style is closely associated with the Italian luxury brand Gucci and is considered a more upscale, fashion-forward version.
  • Driving loafer (also called driving moccasins): A softer, more flexible loafer designed for comfort while driving, often with rubber nubs covering the entire sole.
When and How Are Loafers Worn?

Loafers sit in the smart-casual zone of footwear. They are more polished and formal-looking than sneakers, but less formal than dress shoes like Oxfords (the lace-up shoes worn with suits). This makes them extremely versatile.

You can wear loafers:

  • With jeans and a plain shirt for a relaxed but put-together look
  • With chinos or trousers in a semi-formal or business-casual setting
  • With a blazer for a smart, elegant appearance without being overly formal
  • At the office (in many workplaces), at restaurants, at social gatherings

Loafers are traditionally more associated with men's footwear, but they are very widely worn by all genders today. Leather loafers in dark brown or black are considered classic and timeless.

One popular style choice: wearing loafers without socks or with short, invisible socks (called no-show socks). This gives a clean, minimal, slightly relaxed look. It is especially common in warmer weather.
How the Two Meanings Are Related (Conceptually)

It may seem strange that one word means both "a lazy person" and "a type of shoe," but there is a logical thread. The shoe is called a loafer because it is associated with ease and effortlessness — you don't need to tie laces, you just slip it on and go. It is a shoe for relaxed, leisurely wear. The shoe was named after the idea of loafing around — taking it easy.

So both meanings share the same root idea: ease, relaxation, and lack of effort. The person loafs (does nothing). The shoe lets you slip on without effort. The shoe was literally named after the behavior.

To keep it simple:

  • Loafer (person) = someone who is habitually lazy and avoids work. Slightly disapproving.
  • Loafer (shoe) = a slip-on shoe with no laces, usually leather, worn in casual to smart-casual settings. Comes in several styles (penny, tassel, horsebit, driving).

Both meanings are in active, everyday use. If someone says, "I bought new loafers," they mean the shoe. If someone says, "Stop being a loafer," they mean you're being lazy. Context will always make it clear which meaning is intended.
